title: Name the Variable, Then the Loop

scenes.tts: Charles Blagden went into a room heated to about two hundred degrees Fahrenheit. A thermometer under his tongue read ninety-eight degrees, about one degree above his usual. An egg in hot air heats until it matches the air. A living person did not.
scenes.caption: Charles Blagden went into a room heated to about 200 degrees F. A thermometer under his tongue read 98 degrees, about one degree above his usual. An egg in hot air heats until it matches the air. A living person did not.
scenes.visual: Two level bars in a hot room: the egg's level climbs to the air line, Blagden's tongue thermometer stays near 98 degrees F.
scenes.narration: Charles Blagden went into a room heated to about 200 degrees F. A thermometer under his tongue read 98 degrees, about one degree above his usual. An egg in hot air heats until it matches the air. A living person did not.

scenes.tts: Biologists call this homeostasis, the holding of a body variable within a range compatible with staying alive. Every loop that does it has five parts. The regulated variable is the quantity held, and the set point is its reference value. The sensor measures the variable, and the integrator compares the sensed value with the set point and sends a command. The effector is a muscle, gland or other organ that changes the variable.
scenes.visual: Five chips build into a closed loop: variable, sensor, integrator (with set point), effector, back to the variable; a dot travels round it.
scenes.narration: Biologists call this homeostasis, the holding of a body variable within a range compatible with staying alive. Every loop that does it has five parts. The regulated variable is the quantity held, and the set point is its reference value. The sensor measures the variable, and the integrator compares the sensed value with the set point and sends a command. The effector is a muscle, gland or other organ that changes the variable.

scenes.tts: In an adult human, the variable is core temperature. Temperature sensitive nerve cells in the skin and brain are the sensors. The hypothalamus, a region of the brain, is the integrator. When temperature rises, the effectors are sweat glands, and evaporation of sweat removes heat. When it falls, the effectors include skeletal muscles, which shiver and release heat as they use A T P.

scenes.visual: The loop is relabelled for an adult human; two effector branches appear, sweat glands when temperature rises and skeletal muscles when it falls.

scenes.tts: If temperature rises, sweating brings it down. If it falls, shivering brings it up. Both are negative feedback, because each response pushes the variable back toward the set point. The set point itself can move. In a fever it rises, so a person at normal temperature feels cold and shivers.
scenes.visual: A dot above the set point band is pushed down by a response arrow; a dot below is pushed up; then the band moves up and the dot at the old level is pushed up.

scenes.tts: A regulator holds a variable fairly steady across outside conditions, and a conformer lets it follow the environment. An adult human regulates core temperature. A typical teleost fish in a lake is an ectotherm whose body temperature largely follows the water. That is a different solution, not a lesser one. For blood salt, the shore crab conforms in full-strength seawater and regulates in diluted water.
scenes.visual: A sketch plot of body temperature against outside temperature with a flat human line and a rising fish line, then a crab blood line that follows the water line at one end and stays above it at the other.

scenes.tts: Regulation is not free. In single-housed male mice of one laboratory strain, energy expenditure was about thirty percent higher at twenty-two degrees Celsius than at thirty. A mouse is small and loses heat fast, so at twenty-two degrees it spends more to stay warm. Name the variable first, then the loop that holds it.
